#9781. Building AI Products, Part 1: How To Find AI Use Cases Worth Building in the First Place

Curious about life, whimsical by nature, prone to existential detours and always searching for truth - when laziness doesn't win:)

Curious about life, whimsical by nature, prone to existential detours and always searching for truth - when laziness doesn't win:)

Curious about life, whimsical by nature, prone to existential detours and always searching for truth - when laziness doesn't win:)

In February 2024, Klarna announced its AI assistant was handling two-thirds of customer chats. It was doing the work of 700 agents and cutting resolution time from 11 minutes to 2. It looked like the AI success story everyone wanted. Fifteen months later, Klarna was hiring humans again. The CEO admitted that a focus on cost had led to "lower quality" and customers still wanted a person for complex cases. The AI stayed and alongside people.

So which Klarna got it right: the one that automated 700 agents' worth of work or the one that hired people back? Picture two chats. "Where's my refund?" has one answer, sitting in a database. "Why was I charged twice?" needs someone to hear the customer out and make a call. AI can handle the first on its own. The second needs a person or at least a person checking.

Most AI roadmaps skip that distinction. They list places to add AI, not jobs to split between AI, software and people. The rest of this piece shows how to make that split: a map of where AI value sits, then three tests for any idea. Is it worth it? Is it suitable? How do we build it?

The AI economy has four layers and value grows as you move from answering to doing:

Then run the strategic test: if the AI disappeared tomorrow, what's left?

Each position calls for a different strategy, so know which one you're in before you go further.

Using AI is easy. Earning from it? McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey finds nearly 9 in 10 organisations use AI but only 37% see any EBIT impact(Earnings Before Interest and Taxes) and about 6% earn more than 5% of EBIT from it.

Alexa is the cautionary tale: used daily for timers and weather, rarely for shopping. As one former senior Amazon employee told the Wall Street Journal: "We worried we've hired 10,000 people and we've built a smart timer."

Heavy use doesn't always equal value. And unlike normal software, every AI answer costs money. Whether you charge per seat, per call, per outcome or a hybrid of these, a flat price can lose money on your heaviest users, so model them first.

Before building, run a 60-second TASQ screen:

Next, put a rupee number on it: Value = volume × value per task × automation rate − cost

A support bot handling 50,000 tickets a month, resolving 60% and saving ₹40 each, is worth about ₹9.75 lakh a month after ₹2.25 lakh of AI cost. Note that the AI cost applies to every ticket it attempts, not just the ones it solves. One more catch: if nobody leaves the team, you have freed capacity, not saved cash. Be honest about which one you're claiming.

The useful question to ask is "where should AI sit in this system?" Split the task into parts, then score each part from 1 to 5 on four dimensions:

Use the total to compare ideas. The answer is rarely yes or no.

It's a role: AI can assist (it drafts, a person checks), recommend (it scores, a person decides) or execute (it acts, within set limits). Who should approve a ₹4,500 expense claim? Not the AI. AI reads the receipt, and rules approve it within caps. The pattern that falls out of all this is worth memorising: AI for ambiguity, software for certainty, humans for judgment.

Pick the simplest route that still has lasting value, and stop at the first yes:

Take a WhatsApp bot that refunds up to ₹2,000 for missing food items. Buy the conversational platform. Build the order lookup, per-customer caps, fraud checks and refund rules. Send disputes to a person.

On 2 May 2023, Chegg's share price fell 48% in a day. Students wanted homework help, and ChatGPT gave it free, instantly. When a free AI can do your customer's job, features are no defence.

Here is the whole method as a one-page exercise. Pick one painful, high-volume problem from your work and answer six lines:

Klarna eventually found its balance. By Q3 2025, its CEO said the AI was doing the work of 853 agents, while promising customers that "there will always be a human if you want". That's the lesson in one line: let AI carry the volume and keep people where judgment matters.

#9780. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9779. Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”

Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#9778. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9777. How to Use Message Bus DLQs for Advanced Tail-Based Sampling

Enterprise Integration Architect. Deep diving into Event-Driven Architecture, distributed systems, and OpenTelemetry to build reliable systems.

Enterprise Integration Architect. Deep diving into Event-Driven Architecture, distributed systems, and OpenTelemetry to build reliable systems.

Enterprise Integration Architect. Deep diving into Event-Driven Architecture, distributed systems, and OpenTelemetry to build reliable systems.

Author's Note: The EDA-based architecture introduced in this post is a proposed enterprise implementation pattern and is not part of the official OpenTelemetry Collector reference architecture.

The traditional two-tier OpenTelemetry (OTel) collector architecture can effectively address end-to-end tracing sampling challenges. However, it also introduces significant complexity and is difficult to implement in practice. One of the primary hurdles is the requirement for extremely powerful infrastructure—often necessitating high-performance servers with very large memory capacity—to handle traffic at tens of thousands of spans per second.

A key limitation of this traditional design lies in its point-to-point integration between the tier-1 and tier-2 collectors. This tight coupling forces the tier-2 collectors to independently manage resilience, scalability, and fault tolerance, which adds operational burden and limits flexibility.

In this section, we propose a modern alternative: replacing point-to-point communication with a messaging-based Pub/Sub integration. By decoupling the two tiers through a messaging layer, this approach improves scalability, enhances resilience, and redistributes complexity from collectors to the messaging infrastructure to solve the major challenge of the traditional two-tier OpenTelemetry collector design.

The concept is similar to the Kafka-based buffering approach commonly used in large-scale tracing platforms, where trace collection is decoupled from downstream processing through an intermediary messaging layer.

The proposed architecture introduces an alternative approach to tail-based sampling by externalizing trace buffering and coordination functions from the collector layer to the messaging infrastructure. This design is intended to reduce collector state management requirements while providing additional flexibility for scalability, resiliency, and operational deployment. The following sections describe the architecture, implementation options, benefits, and associated trade-offs.

The architecture is built around an event mesh that provides both reliable trace transport and temporary persistence.

The event mesh is a virtual messaging infrastructure built on top of the underlying network. It is formed by a collection of interconnected message buses that work together as a unified event distribution layer.

The message bus is responsible not only for routing data between tier-1 and tier-2 collectors but also for providing a persistent storage layer for the incoming trace. This design removes the need for tier-2 collectors to cache all spans belonging to the same trace. Instead, the message bus temporarily retains the data, allowing tier-2 collectors to consume and process it in batches before forwarding it to the APM backend.

There are three major components in this architecture design

Compared with traditional tail-based architecture, this solution only requires enhanced communication between the tier-1 and tier-2 collectors to support the message bus.

Similar to a traditional two-tier OpenTelemetry (OTel) Collector architecture, the tier-1 collectors are distributed across application hosts or deployed on dedicated collector servers in different network segments isolated by firewalls. These collectors connect to a message bus configured in an active-standby topology to provide high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR) capabilities.

The tier-2 collectors are deployed within the same network segment and consume data from the message bus. As a result, there is no need to deploy a dedicated load balancer in front of the tier-2 collectors, since message distribution and failover are handled by the message bus infrastructure.

This solution adopts a two-tier collector design, with communication between the collector tiers facilitated through the message bus. Redis is optionally used as an in-memory cache to store global trace IDs and their associated metadata. This solution also introduces some extra optional services to decouple the function from the tier-2 collector.

The solution consists of three core components and three optional components, as described below:

Within the event mesh, the message bus serves as the fundamental building block. Its role extends beyond simply transporting trace data between tier-1 and tier-2 collectors. By leveraging messaging capabilities such as routing, filtering, buffering, and protocol abstraction, the message bus processes and distributes messages to the appropriate consumers. This allows the message bus to distribute trace data efficiently while reducing the complexity of the application logic required by the tier-2 collectors, thereby improving the scalability and maintainability of the overall solution.

The OpenTelemetry (OTel) Collector consists of three main components: receivers, processors, and exporters.

In this architecture, the tier-1 collector receives traces from application SDKs or third-party products through its receivers. The traces are then pre-processed by the processors before being published to a message bus and forwarded to the tier-2 collector.

The OTLP receiver and exporter support gRPC and HTTP, and the contrib repository provides messaging-specific components — including a Kafka receiver and exporter, and a Solace receiver for broker-generated trace events. Depending on the chosen message bus, integration may therefore require configuration of existing components rather than custom implementations; a custom exporter is required only where no component exists for the target broker. In addition, the processor component must be enhanced to read and update trace metadata and global configuration parameters, such as sampling-strategy settings, from Redis or another persistent data store.

In many deployments, organizations use vendor-specific agents instead of tier-1 OpenTelemetry Collectors. As a result, it is necessary either to enhance the vendor agents to publish trace data to the message bus directly or to introduce an additional collector layer that acts as the tier-1 collector and receives telemetry data from these agents before forwarding it to the message bus.

This design relies on the Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) functionality of the message bus. The tier-1 collector sends trace spans to the message bus, and the message can then be retrieved from the DLQ after 30 seconds.

The tier-1 collector ingests trace spans from applications and third-party products and publishes them to dedicated message-bus topics (otel_trace/[trace_id]). Each message (trace span) must include the following mandatory header fields:

The data queue’s subscription rule is as follows:

The tier-2 collector monitors Dead Letter Queue and uses the first expired root span as a trigger to process the corresponding trace. It retrieves all spans sharing the same trace ID from both the active queue and the dead message queue through selector-based filtering. The complete trace is then evaluated against the configured sampling rules. Qualified traces are batched and forwarded to the APM backend, while unqualified traces are discarded.

This design leverages the queue Time-to-Live (TTL) and Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) to achieve the same objective as the buffer window used in traditional tail-based sampling. When a tier-2 collector consumes a message from the control queue, it can be assured that all spans generated within the preceding 30-second window have already been persisted in the data queue. The buffer duration is configurable and can be adjusted dynamically, with changes taking effect immediately.

#9776. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9775. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9774. When AI Character Chat Feels Flat: Fixing Repetition, Soft Refusals, and Lost Plot Threads

A chat that felt electric on message three can feel hollow by message thirty. The character loops the same compliment. Soft refusals appear where the scene should continue. A plot thread you planted yesterday vanishes. That flatness is rarely "the model is dumb." It is usually weak steering, missing continuity hooks, and an app that does not surface the right memory or regenerate controls.

This guide is a repair manual for three failure modes—repetition, soft refusals, and lost plot threads—so you can diagnose fast and fix without throwing away a good persona. It is for anyone comparing ai character chat apps who wants scenes that stay sharp past the honeymoon messages.

People say "flat" for different bugs. Separate them before you rewrite the card:

Write down which of the three failed. Then apply the matching fix.

Repetition is the most common complaint and the most fixable. Models love high-probability phrasing. Your job is to break the attractor without flooding the context.

Run three user turns that should force variety: a sudden obstacle, a yes/no question, and a silence ("I don't answer; I just wait."). Score whether wording and tactics change. Apps that still clone their last paragraph after that are weak on diversity—one reason people keep a shortlist of character ai alternatives.

Soft refusals are slippery. They are not always a hard block screen. They look like therapist speech in a noir bar, "healthier choices" mid-heist, sudden amnesia about a dark beat you already established inside allowed settings, or endless clarifying questions instead of committing to an action.

Sometimes that is correct—your request crossed a real boundary. Often it is over-refusal: the model hedges because the prompt is ambiguous, the card conflicts with the latest user line, or the app's safety layer is twitchy even in fiction mode.

If the answer is a forgotten filter, flip the control and retry. No clever prompt beats a toggle.

On Pogee, treat boundary settings and persona setup as one workflow: lock what the character will and will not do, then play. Fighting a soft refusal every message means adjust controls or switch tools—not write a longer apology prompt.

Respect hard stops that match your ethics and platform rules. Soft-refusal repair is for when the model refuses tone and commitment inside content you already configured as allowed. Do not jailbreak safety systems; do remove ambiguity and accidental assistant framing.

Plot loss feels personal—"they forgot our promise"—but it is usually mechanics: context filled with banter so early clues fell off, no pinned summary of open threads, a scene jump without a carry-forward line, or regenerates that drop facts you never restated.

Maintain three to seven bullets somewhere the model can see (pinned note, author's note, lore field, or paste at session start):

Update when a beat resolves. Delete dead threads. Bloated memory fields cause as much amnesia as empty ones.

Skip the five-paragraph recap rant. Use a surgical patch:

(OOC: Restore continuity: the envelope initials match the clerk; limp unchanged; buyer name "Harbor Owl." Continue from the alley, do not restart.)

Then your in-character line should reference one fact so the model has to use it. If they still invent a new plot, export what you care about and reopen with the ledger at the top.

Pass = both facts survive. Partial = one survives. Fail = fanfic reboot. Use that score when you evaluate platforms, not the splash animation.

That checklist turns "it feels flat" into actionable edits and makes A/B tests fair when you bounce between tools.

Build the repair habits first; then pick the app that makes them cheap. Roundups of ai character chat apps are more useful when you score repetition recovery, refusal clarity, and plot retention—not avatar quality alone.

Flat AI character chat is usually repairable. Break repetition with new beats and structural constraints. Handle soft refusals by clarifying fiction frame, aligning the card, and using real content controls—or by moving to a better-fitting tool. Rescue lost plots with a tiny open-thread ledger and surgical OOC restores instead of rage rewrites.

Practice those three repairs on any platform. Then judge character ai alternatives by how rarely you need the repairs—and how fast they work when you do. When compliments stop looping, the character commits to the beat you allowed, and yesterday's envelope still matters in tonight's alley, the chat stops feeling flat. It starts feeling directed.

#9773. Your Startup's Biggest Security Vulnerability Isn't Your Code — It's You

25+ year entrepreneur, real estate investor & M&A/turnaround specialist. Bestselling author of "The Influence of Military Strategies to Busi

25+ year entrepreneur, real estate investor & M&A/turnaround specialist. Bestselling author of "The Influence of Military Strategies to Busi

25+ year entrepreneur, real estate investor & M&A/turnaround specialist. Bestselling author of "The Influence of Military Strategies to Busi

Alright folks, I’m going to tell you something your dev team already knows but is too polite to say to your face: the biggest security hole in your company isn’t in your codebase. It’s sitting in the founder’s chair.

I’ve spent 25+ years in business warfare — buying troubled companies, turning them around, doing private security consulting, and researching cybersecurity from the operator’s side, not the engineer’s. And I can tell you this with total confidence: when small businesses get hacked, it’s almost never some hoodie-wearing genius cracking encryption. It’s a founder reusing a password. It’s an admin clicking a link. It’s someone handing over the keys because the “IT guy” on the phone sounded convincing.

Here’s the part that should scare you straight. The average cost of a data breach for a small business runs into six figures — and a huge percentage of small businesses that suffer a major breach shut down within months. Not because the hack was sophisticated. Because the recovery was impossible.

Think about it like a military campaign. You’ve built this beautiful fortress — your product, your customer list, your payment systems. And then you leave the back gate open with a sign that says “come on in.” That’s what a reused password is. That’s what an unpatched laptop is. That’s what your executive assistant’s inbox is when nobody’s trained her what a spear-phishing email looks like.

The attackers know this. They’re not wasting zero-days on your seed-stage SaaS. They’re running the cheapest playbook in the book: find the human, fool the human, own the human.

After decades of watching businesses get hit, the pattern is always the same. Different companies, different industries, same five failures:

1. Password reuse across everything. Your founder uses the same password for the company AWS account and some forum he joined in 2019. That forum gets breached, the credentials get sold, and now someone’s logging into your infrastructure at 3 AM. One password, total compromise. This is the single most common way in, and it takes ten minutes to fix with a password manager.

2. No multi-factor authentication on the crown jewels. Email, banking, cloud infrastructure, domain registrar — if these don’t have MFA, you’re one phished password away from losing the company. Your domain registrar alone: if an attacker takes your domain, they own your email, your password resets, everything.

3. Nobody trained the team. Your people are your perimeter. One well-crafted email pretending to be you, asking your bookkeeper to “wire this quickly before the call,” and the money’s gone. I’ve seen it happen to companies with real revenue and real investors. The fix isn’t a $50,000 security audit — it’s a 30-minute training and a culture where nobody wires money on an email request. Ever.

4. The founder’s personal accounts are the backdoor. Here’s the espionage angle: attackers don’t target your company directly. They target you. Your personal email, your social media, your kid’s school portal — anything that can be used for leverage, impersonation, or password-reset chains. If your personal Gmail is the recovery email for your business accounts, your personal security IS your business security.

5. No incident plan. When — not if — something happens, the first hour decides everything. Most founders have no plan: no idea who to call, no backups verified, no idea which accounts to lock down first. Panic is not a strategy. A one-page incident plan written on a calm Tuesday beats a brilliant response improvised during a breach.

Here’s where my background kicks in. In military doctrine, you don’t defend everywhere equally — you defend what matters, and you think like the enemy.

Ask yourself: if I were trying to rob my own company, how would I do it? You’d go after the email first (it’s the master key to every password reset). Then the money (banking, payment processors). Then the customers (their data is your liability). Work backward from there and harden in that order.

This is threat modeling, and you don’t need to be technical to do it. You need to be honest. Most founders aren’t.

You don’t need a security team. You need discipline on the basics — the boring stuff that stops 90% of attacks:

None of this requires an engineer. All of it requires a founder who takes security personally — because the attacker already does.

Cybersecurity isn’t an IT problem for founders. It’s a leadership problem. Your company will never be more secure than your own habits, because you hold the keys to everything.

The good news? The basics work. The attackers are lazy — they’re going after the companies that left the gate open. Close the gate, lock it properly, and they’ll move on to someone easier. That’s not paranoia. That’s just good business warfare.

Want the full field manual? I put together a free 20-Point Cyber Hygiene Checklist — the exact basics above, expanded into a one-page audit you can run on your company this afternoon: https://therealmdwhite.gumroad.com/l/iokmxh

And if you want the complete playbook — threat modeling, incident response plans, vendor security, the works — my Cybersecurity for Non-Technical Founders guide covers it: https://therealmdwhite.gumroad.com/l/ccalsf

#9772. I built a language model that only learns when someone pays $2.49

Most AI labs take their training data for free and charge you for the output. I wanted to see what happens if you flip that. You pay for the input, and the output is free.

The result is brAIAIn, a parody AI lab with a real model behind it. The model knows exactly what people have paid to tell it, and nothing else. Each sentence someone buys becomes a new model version, with its own release notes, a research paper, a status page incident, and benchmark scores. It currently has 476 parameters and scores 0.0% on GSM8K.

The joke only works if the machinery is real, so here is how it runs. It runs on no servers, no database, no webhooks, and a hosting bill of $0.

A webhook needs something always listening, and I didn't want to run a server. So the workflow runs on a schedule, every 10 minutes. It asks the Stripe API for completed Checkout Sessions on the Payment Link, using a restricted Stripe key.

A sentence arrives as a custom field on the checkout. The trainer:

Retraining everything on every run sounds wasteful, but the whole model is smaller than this article. It also means that removing a sentence actually removes it, from every version, on the next run. There is no "the weights remember."

GitHub's scheduler is often late, sometimes by a lot. An external free cron service calls the workflow_dispatch endpoint as a backup, so a purchase usually goes live within minutes.

It is a word-level trigram model with backoff. That is a count of which word follows each pair of words, and of which word follows each single word for when it has never seen the pair.

The "parameters" on the spec sheet are real. They are the number of distinct word pairs and triples it has counted.

Two details make it feel more like a real lab's model than it has any right to:

The trained model is exported as a small JSON file. The chat page loads it and samples from it in JavaScript:

It generates eight candidates and keeps the one that shares the most words with your question. That is the entire "alignment" layer. It does not understand the question. It is just more likely to repeat some of it back, which in fairness is also how a lot of meetings work.

Inference costs nothing because your laptop is the GPU.

The trainer runs each version on a handful of real benchmark questions, including GSM8K grade-school math. It reports the score next to the best published scores from real model papers, with sources. brAIAIn scores 0.0%. The site has a side-by-side page showing each problem, the correct answer, and what brAIAIn said instead.

Lifetime revenue so far is $10. The unit economics are excellent, because the unit is a sentence and the cost of goods is zero.

Ask it something at braiain.com. The answer will be confident and wrong. If you want it to know something, it is $2.49, and you get release notes.

The code, the corpus, and every version are public in the repo.

Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.
