#9771. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9770. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9769. Dead Code in Flutter Is More Than an Analyzer Warning

Finding an unused_element warning is easy. Deciding whether a file is safe to delete is not.

Flutter applications have several legitimate ways to use code without an obvious direct reference: generated registries, route tables, dependency injection, conditional imports, flavors, platform channels, annotations, test-only helpers, and public package exports. A search that returns zero references is useful evidence, but it is not a verdict.

That distinction led me to build flutter-dead-code-audit, an open-source Agent Skill for auditing unused Dart declarations and potentially orphaned .dart files through a review-first workflow.

Repository: github.com/LucasMenezeslc/flutter-dead-code-audit

The Dart analyzer is excellent at detecting local issues such as:

But repository cleanup also involves broader questions:

A tool that ignores these questions may produce a convincing report and still recommend the wrong deletion.

Consider a field that is assigned in several lifecycle callbacks but never read:

Mechanically, the field is write-only. Removing the declaration alone is not enough; every assignment must also be removed for the code to compile.

However, there is a more important product question: was the field abandoned, or was a missing read supposed to control replay, analytics, persistence, or UI state?

The correct finding is therefore not automatically “safe cleanup.” It may be:

The field is write-only in the current code, but product intent is unresolved.

That is why the workflow separates mechanical evidence from human decisions.

Audit mode is read-only. The bundled scripts combine:

The result is a list of candidates, not an automatic deletion list.

Candidates are presented in small groups. Each receives one of three decisions:

Retained code remains visible in later reports. It is not silently ignored, which prevents the same investigation from being repeated every few months.

Cleanup is allowed only for candidates explicitly approved as remove. Removals are applied in small batches, followed by analyzer and test verification.

After cleanup, the report suggests behavior-oriented checks based on the affected area. Removing a playback field, for example, should result in a playback test checklist rather than only a green static analyzer result.

Static correctness is necessary, but it does not prove that supported behavior survived.

A high-confidence finding should normally have at least two independent signals and cleared false-positive checks.

The evidence hierarchy used by the skill is:

When signals conflict, confidence goes down. The workflow does not average the conflict away.

Large raw lists are difficult to review. The report therefore groups findings into:

Every candidate preserves its location, evidence, checks, confidence, risk, recommendation, and verification command. The executive view stays compact while detailed evidence remains available when needed.

From the root of a Flutter or Dart project:

The scripts require Python 3.10 or newer and use only the Python standard library. Dart can come from PATH or FVM. Script output uses relative paths so reports do not expose the absolute project directory.

It also does not install project tooling, rewrite analyzer rules, or hand-delete generated files during an audit.

The project is MIT licensed and open to contributions. The most useful feedback is a small reproducible Flutter or Dart example that exposes a false positive, a false negative, or a dynamic usage pattern that is not yet modeled.

If you have encountered dead code hidden behind routing, dependency injection, code generation, conditional imports, platform implementations, or package exports, I would like to learn from that case.

Templates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.

#9768. Código morto em Flutter é mais do que um warning do analyzer

Encontrar um warning unused_element é fácil. Decidir se um arquivo pode ser apagado com segurança não é.

Aplicações Flutter possuem várias formas legítimas de usar código sem uma referência direta óbvia: registries gerados, tabelas de rotas, injeção de dependências, imports condicionais, flavors, platform channels, annotations, helpers exclusivos de testes e exports públicos de packages. Uma busca que retorna zero referências é uma evidência útil, mas não é um veredito.

Essa diferença me levou a criar a flutter-dead-code-audit, uma Agent Skill open source para auditar declarações Dart sem uso e arquivos .dart potencialmente órfãos por meio de um fluxo que exige revisão antes da remoção.

Repositório: github.com/LucasMenezeslc/flutter-dead-code-audit

O analyzer do Dart é excelente para encontrar problemas locais como:

Mas uma limpeza de repositório também precisa responder perguntas mais amplas:

Uma ferramenta que ignora essas perguntas pode produzir um relatório convincente e ainda recomendar a remoção errada.

Considere um campo que recebe valores em diferentes callbacks, mas nunca é lido:

Mecanicamente, o campo é write-only. Remover apenas a declaração não basta; todas as atribuições também precisam ser removidas para o código continuar compilando.

Existe, porém, uma pergunta de produto mais importante: o campo foi abandonado ou faltou uma leitura que deveria controlar replay, analytics, persistência ou estado visual?

Portanto, a conclusão correta não é automaticamente “cleanup seguro”. Ela pode ser:

O campo é write-only no código atual, mas a intenção de produto ainda não foi resolvida.

Por isso o fluxo separa evidência mecânica de decisão humana.

O modo Audit é somente leitura. Os scripts combinam:

O resultado é uma lista de candidatos, não uma lista automática de exclusão.

Os candidatos são apresentados em grupos pequenos. Cada um recebe uma decisão:

Código mantido continua visível em relatórios futuros. Ele não é silenciosamente ignorado, evitando que a mesma investigação seja repetida alguns meses depois.

O Cleanup só pode alterar candidatos explicitamente aprovados como remove. As mudanças são aplicadas em lotes pequenos e seguidas por analyzer e testes.

Depois da limpeza, o relatório sugere verificações de comportamento com base na área afetada. A remoção de um campo de playback, por exemplo, deve gerar um checklist do fluxo de reprodução — não apenas um analyzer verde.

Correção estática é necessária, mas não prova que o comportamento suportado foi preservado.

Um candidato de alta confiança normalmente precisa de pelo menos dois sinais independentes e de verificações de falso positivo concluídas.

Quando os sinais entram em conflito, a confiança diminui. O fluxo não esconde o conflito atrás de uma média.

Listas enormes são difíceis de revisar. Por isso, os resultados são agrupados em:

Cada candidato preserva localização, evidências, verificações, confiança, risco, recomendação e comando de validação. A visão executiva permanece compacta, enquanto os detalhes ficam disponíveis quando necessários.

Depois, comece com uma solicitação somente leitura:

Os scripts exigem Python 3.10 ou superior e utilizam apenas a biblioteca padrão. O Dart pode vir do PATH ou do FVM. A saída utiliza caminhos relativos para não expor o diretório absoluto do projeto nos relatórios.

Ela também não instala ferramentas no projeto, não altera regras do analyzer e não remove arquivos gerados diretamente durante uma auditoria.

O projeto usa licença MIT e está aberto a contribuições. O feedback mais útil é um exemplo Flutter ou Dart pequeno e reproduzível que revele um falso positivo, um falso negativo ou uma forma de uso dinâmico ainda não modelada.

Se você já encontrou código aparentemente morto escondido por rotas, injeção de dependências, codegen, imports condicionais, implementações de plataforma ou exports públicos, quero conhecer esse caso.

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9766. Hindsight-Driven Development: An Iterative Approach to Building Software With AI

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI scientist, builder, and computer science faculty member.

AI makes trying cheaper than guessing, yet spec-driven development still asks you to guess first. Meet Hindsight-Driven Development.

You spend two hours writing a detailed spec for a feature. An AI coding agent builds it in ten minutes. You try it, and within a minute you see what the spec got wrong.

In those same two hours, you could have built it, tried it, thrown away three versions, and kept the fourth.

Specs force us to make our most detailed decisions at the moment we know the least.

For decades, that was a fair trade. Building was expensive, so we paid to describe software first.

AI broke that trade. Yet a popular response to AI coding agents is spec-driven development. Tools like GitHub’s Spec Kit and Amazon’s Kiro have you write and sign off on requirements, a design, and a task list before the agent writes any code. More detail, decided earlier. That gets it backward.

Writing detailed specs for AI agents is waterfall, rebranded for the AI era.

Even when that spec gets edited later, you still decide before you see.

One exception, which I’ll come back to: decide up front whatever is expensive to undo. Build everything else.

Writing a spec means imagining a product that doesn’t exist yet and simulating it all in your head. That takes three kinds of guessing:

No amount of good writing fixes this. Imagination has limits. People don’t know what they want until they see what they don’t want. Yet the spec gets reviewed, approved, and signed off, and the guess gains an authority it never earned.

A spec can be perfectly clear, perfectly consistent, and completely wrong.

If you’ve ever shipped a feature exactly as specified and watched people ignore it, you already know the problem.

We get very good at building what we imagined, and never find out what we actually needed.

Agile admitted part of this problem. But building was still expensive. Three versions of one feature, just to see which felt right? Rarely worth the cost.

So the spec survived as user stories, tickets, and acceptance criteria. Agile shortened the distance between guessing and feedback. You still had to guess first.

Say you’re building a customer-support assistant. Should it ask two questions or five? Suggest a fix early, or wait? Will it feel helpful or pushy? Skip the meeting. Generate one and talk to it.

The first version asks too many questions, forgets what you told it, and jumps to answers too early. You see all three in minutes, and they produce better requirements than anything you’d write in advance.

You might say AI can write the spec in ten minutes too. It can, but only what you already imagine, and the limit was never typing. A faster spec is still a guess.

I call this Hindsight-Driven Development. A spec asks you to decide with foresight, before anything exists. This approach lets you decide with hindsight, after you’ve seen the real thing.

Start with one sentence of intent. Build a rough version, use it, and keep correcting it until it does what you want. The fastest hindsight comes from a real user, so put the rough version in front of one early. The corrections sound like this:

“This workflow is confusing.” “Don’t offer a refund before I’ve finished explaining.” “Show me three different approaches.”

Nobody writes “don’t offer a refund before I’ve finished explaining” into a spec. Everyone says it the first time the bot does it.

The third one matters most: asking for several approaches early stops you from polishing only the first idea.

Predicting what’s right is hard. Recognizing what’s wrong is easy. This approach trades the hard problem for the easy one.

Agile still writes each ticket first. Here, the product writes the next one.

And vibe coding accepts whatever the AI produces and moves on. Hindsight-Driven Development questions every result, corrects it, and keeps every correction as a test or a line in the spec.

Fred Brooks wrote “plan to throw one away” in 1975, then later called that too simple. His better lesson, from 1986: “grow, not build, software.”

Slack began as the in-house chat tool of a team building an online game. The game failed. The tool became the product. The idea is old. What changed is the price.

A prototype used to be a project. Now it’s a prompt.

They do. But a spec written in advance can’t cover a gap nobody knew was there.

Agents drift less from forgetting than from decisions we haven’t made yet.

When the agent guesses wrong, you see it the first time you use the product, and the fix costs minutes. That fix then goes into the tests, and the spec the agent reads next time.

What’s harmful is the spec written first, from foresight, by people asked to imagine what they can’t yet see. Hindsight-Driven Development flips the order: the spec comes last, from what the team has already seen.

Each person corrects the product from their own angle. Only the version you keep goes through code review, and the decisions behind it go into the spec. The ones you throw away cost a few minutes and nothing else.

Every checkable correction becomes an automated test, like “it should remember my order number.” A correction like “this feels confusing” stays a note in the spec until someone decides what better looks like. AI merges it all into one readable spec, flags where people disagree, and asks the team to settle it.

Nobody writes the spec. Everyone shapes it, and AI keeps it whole.

The testable parts stay matched to the product, because a test fails the moment they drift apart. The team aligns around the spec, and the agents read it too, so they stop guessing.

Spec-driven development with extra steps? The document may look the same, but here it records what people saw, not what they imagined.

And the risks no demo reveals, like security holes or failure under heavy load? You don’t guess those either. You inherit the rules others learned the hard way, and test for them. For everything else, workflows, features, and behavior nobody predicted, you discover it by building.

The exception I promised at the start: anything other people build on, like an API another team uses, a customer contract, or anything a regulator requires, is expensive to undo, so agree it up front. That list is short. Most of what a product does sits outside it.

AI now handles much of the slow part: writing the code. The bottleneck becomes deciding what to build, and that’s a job for the whole team: product, engineering, and architecture.

Even architecture works this way. A good design is never written in one go. It starts rough and gets refined, round after round. Until now, all that refining happened on paper. Now the architect refines the working product itself.

The scarce skill now is knowing what’s wrong when you see it.

We spent fifty years getting better at describing software before building it. That made sense when every line took real effort.

That’s no longer true. When a working version of a feature costs minutes, a detailed spec written before a single experiment is premature commitment dressed up as diligence.

For decades, we built with foresight. Now we can build with hindsight.

What’s the biggest thing your spec got wrong that you only saw once the product ran? Tell me in the responses. And if you think I’m wrong, tell me why.

#9764. Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 21st of October 2026 11:26 AM

i discovered this blog two months back from the idscan/Nexus story and was immediately impressed by the journalism on here. as soon as i heard about this doing the rounds elsewhere on social media my first instinct was “i wonder if krebs has written about it yet?” and lo and behold. well anyways, great work as usual, cheers

Maybe I should have kept my blog as pure HTML, perhaps with some perl, instead of going to WordPress.

Just don’t forget the cgi-perl and imagemaps.

Hugo, yes! I finally retired my old Drupal-based site last week and switched to Hugo. For my blog-like site, it’s perfect and saves cost, since it’s served as a static site.

The vulnerabilities can hardly be referred to as zero-days. They have been known to The PHP Foundation from 2024 but people decided that other bugs were more urgent.

Thanks for the heads-up. I run a small film site on PHP and found out about this from your post, not from my host. If you’re on shared hosting, it’s worth opening a ticket and asking which PHP build they’re actually running instead of trusting the control panel: the version shown there isn’t always the one serving requests.

#9763. Week Ahead: November 17 Brings 6,613 Scheduled Layoffs as November Stays Heavy

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at layoffatlas.com

The week of November 17, 2026, is shaping up as one of the heaviest layoff weeks of the fall. According to current WARN data tracked by Layoff Atlas, 6,613 workers are scheduled to be affected that week — the third-heaviest week on the upcoming calendar, behind only the weeks of November 24 (9,300 workers) and November 10 (6,887 workers).

November is not letting up. Across the six weeks from November 3 through December 8, a total of 28,844 workers are scheduled for layoffs. The November 17 week alone accounts for nearly a quarter of that total, and it sits in the middle of a three-week stretch — November 10, November 17, and November 24 — in which more than 22,000 workers are scheduled to be affected.

Here is how the upcoming calendar looks, by effective week:

The pattern is worth noting. The current week, November 3, is comparatively quiet at 2,350 workers. Then the numbers roughly triple for three straight weeks before falling back sharply in December. Do not mistake the quiet start of November for a quiet month: the bulk of the month's scheduled layoffs is still ahead.

These figures come from the 90-day WARN window, which currently holds 666 notices covering 62,948 reported workers, with 28 notices where no worker count was available. That window rolls forward daily, so the totals shift as new notices are filed and older ones age out.

California and Washington continue to dominate the national picture. California leads with 18,196 reported workers in the window, followed by Washington with 17,336. Together, the two states account for more than half of all reported workers nationwide. Illinois (3,649), Texas (2,978), and Maryland (2,429) round out the top five.

Maryland's presence in the top five is itself a recent shift — Virginia held the fifth spot a day earlier. State rankings move for mundane reasons as often as dramatic ones: a single large filing can lift a state, and the rolling window drops older filings daily. A one-place change is a signal to watch, not a verdict on a state's economy.

These state totals are also not a census of layoffs. They reflect only notices that were filed, published, and captured by connected sources, and reporting rules vary by state. Some states publish promptly and completely; others publish little or nothing. Missing source coverage is not zero layoffs.

The pipeline behind these weekly totals is still active. The most recent dated filings on the registry include GEICO's 114-worker notice in Lakeland, Florida, and International Automotive Components Group's 83-worker notice in Cottondale, Alabama — both filed November 2 and effective December 31, 2026. Alaska Airlines filed a 121-worker notice covering Seattle, Spokane, and Renton, Washington, on October 30, also effective December 31. Pharmaceutics International filed a 94-worker notice for Hunt Valley, Maryland, on October 30, effective December 29.

Most of those new filings point to late December rather than mid-November, which is normal: WARN notices are typically filed weeks before the effective date, so today's filings shape December's calendar while November's was largely set weeks ago.

A few cautions apply to this number, as they do to every WARN total:

First, these are reported plans, not confirmed job losses. A WARN notice is an employer's advance notification of a planned mass layoff or plant closure. Some planned layoffs are later reduced, delayed, or cancelled, and some workers find other roles with the same employer. The notice is the best public signal available, but it is not a final count of people who lose their jobs.

Second, the weekly totals group workers by effective date, not by notice date. A worker counted in the November 17 week may have received notice in September or October. The week tells you when the job loss is scheduled to take effect, not when it was announced.

Third, the totals exclude the 28 notices in the window with no reported worker count. The true number of affected workers is therefore somewhat higher than 6,613 for that week and 62,948 overall — by an amount that cannot be computed from the published data.

Two things will determine whether November stays this heavy: the December calendar, where new late-December filings are arriving daily, and the week of November 24 itself — currently the heaviest at 9,300 workers — where any filings that slip or shrink would bring the month's total down.

For workers with a November 17 effective date, the practical steps are the same as for any WARN notice: confirm the effective date and whether the layoff is permanent or temporary, check unemployment eligibility in your state, and review health coverage options before the last day. State rapid-response teams, triggered by WARN filings, can help with job search and retraining — and they are free.

We will keep tracking the weekly totals as they change. The November wave is real, it is concentrated in three weeks, and the middle of it arrives November 17.

#9762. Four Relationships, One Second Brain: What You Need to Know

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Building shared memory for AI agents. Writing Super Second Brain on memory, identity, and human agency.

Once fidelity becomes high enough, one day you hear something like this.

“On this issue, I think I know you better than you know yourself.”

People do not respond to those words in the same way. Some laugh, some take offense, and some hurt for a long time.

I read that difference along two axes I have used in earlier whitepapers.

The two axes are independent. Some people can bear reality without seeing it well; others see it well but struggle to bear it. That gives us four rooms.

Of the four rooms, ④ looks the most peaceful from the outside. The owner is satisfied, the AI complies, and there is no conflict. The second brain tells its owner what they want to hear with increasing sophistication. The uncomfortable things other people used to say are filtered out by the agent before they arrive.

Room ③ is noisy, but it moves. Pain means something is being seen, and someone who sees can make changes. As experiences of being wrong without falling apart accumulate, ③ moves toward ①.

Room ② is comfortable, and that is where it stops. In terms of the steps in Chapter 4, it has skipped the mirror and gone straight to the representative. The work runs well. But the person that the second brain comes to resemble is less the actual owner than the owner as described by the owner.

I do not want this table used to label people. The same person may be in ① at work and ③ with family. After a week without enough sleep, anyone can slide toward ④. I do, too.

The four rooms do not classify kinds of people. They are a hypothesis about the relationship someone has with a second brain in a particular domain and state. As in my earlier whitepapers, the principle is to look for recurring patterns rather than judge from a single scene.

The same second brain becomes another self for one person, an assistant for another, a mirror for another, and a mechanism for automating self-deception for another.

The two table images reproduce the existing English translation of the author’s original tables. The Korean originals are included in the review package. This essay is part of the ongoing Super Second Brain whitepaper.

If AI Shares Your Memories and Values, Are You Still the Original?

#9761. nemotron-halloween

TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.

I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.

That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.

The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.

A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.

Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.

While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.

The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.

The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.

Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.

The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.

After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison.

If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.

It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.

Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.

Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.

With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.

Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.

A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.

NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.

Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.

To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.

Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)

Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.

The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.

The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.

Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.

For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin and ghost outfits. That is the sort of visual context I want the house to use. Apparently even livestock have more elaborate Halloween plans than I do.

Five very woolly trick-or-treaters in a synthetic test replay. Costume labels come from the saved Omni analysis; boxes and track IDs are illustrative.

The sheep are a synthetic test, not evidence of a successful Halloween night. Real driveway groups, costumes and night lighting still need testing. Detection does trigger automatic greetings, but I fear trendy costume identification and suitably witty retorts may need some post training. Since the house has no eyes, he calls his visitor awareness echolocation. I am letting him have that one.

There is more to do: the animation can always improve, complete performance testing needs real visitors, and candy will one day be provided automatically. I have not yet reached the original goal of leaving him to run Halloween while I head off with my family to see the other neighborhood ghouls. But that is still the point of all this. One day a child will meet a grumpy old house, try a little kindness and discover that the old timber has a soft spot. And gives out candy bars.

The MonsterHouse code itself is not packaged for release, but every NVIDIA model it uses is available today, and the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent gets you most of the way. This is the path I would follow.

A cached response bank and saved audio for your most common lines will make even a slow monster feel quick. In fact, if you happen to be limited by computing power, there is no reason why you can’t have a Live version that just uses Nemotron 3 ASR, a python conversation router, with all cached audio. You can use the Bolt E4B and Magpie pipeline to generate 100s of responses offline, then use the cache for the show. I’ll be doing this for the interactive pumpkins.

#9760. Moonwell Exploit: A Donation That Skipped the MAMO Cap

Posted on Nov 3 • Originally published at panda-security.xyz

Originally published at Moonwell Exploit: A Donation That Skipped the MAMO Cap

On 27 August 2026, an attacker borrowed $11,028,762 of cbBTC, WETH, USDC and wstETH from Moonwell, a Compound v2 style lending market on Base. The collateral behind those loans was MAMO, a thinly traded token that the attacker had formally deposited for only about $160K. Around 8.73M USDC of the proceeds left Base through Circle's CCTP within the hour, which is where the "$8.7M exploit" headline comes from.

The case is back in the news because on 2 November 2026 Certora published a formal verification write-up of the bug, and it is worth studying closely. The market had a supply cap that was meant to stop exactly this kind of oversized collateral position. The cap was set correctly and it measured the right number. It simply never ran, because the attacker added most of the collateral with a plain ERC-20 transfer instead of a deposit.

This post explains how the attack worked, why the cap did not fire, why this is the third Compound fork hit by the same pattern in 2026, and what we check for in lending code during an audit.

Moonwell listed MAMO through proposal MIP-B48 on 15 October 2025 with a 50% collateral factor, a 20,000,000 MAMO supply cap, a 3,000,000 MAMO borrow cap and a 30% reserve factor. According to Certora, the listing note from Anthias said roughly $200K of MAMO could be sold instantly while keeping slippage below the 7% liquidation bonus. In other words, the cap existed to keep MAMO collateral close to what liquidators could actually sell. On the morning of the attack, 20M MAMO was worth about $212K.

Like every Compound v2 fork, Moonwell gives suppliers a receipt token. One mMAMO is redeemable for an amount of MAMO set by the exchange rate:

Moonwell's own functions update totalBorrows, totalReserves and totalSupply. The fourth input, totalCash, is not stored. It is read live from the token, as Certora quotes from MErc20.sol:

That single line is the whole vulnerability. Anything that increases the contract's MAMO balance increases what every existing mMAMO is worth, whether or not it came through Moonwell.

Anthias Labs' post-mortem traces the funding back to 800.098 ETH withdrawn from Tornado Cash on 21 and 23 August. A linked account sold 799 ETH for 1,947,391 USDC through CoW Swap, bridged it to Base and handed MAMO, USDC and gas to the principal account (0x719e...919D, shown truncated in the post-mortem). From there, all times are UTC on 27 August:

The formal deposit of 15.09M MAMO stayed below the 20M cap, so every mint passed. It gave the attacker roughly 735.6M mMAMO, about three quarters of all mMAMO in existence. That share matters: whoever owns most of the receipts captures most of any increase in the exchange rate.

The two direct transfers added 53,393,290 MAMO to the market. No Mint event was emitted and mMAMO total supply did not change, but cash did. Anthias measured the exchange rate rising from about 0.020513 to 0.075460 MAMO per mMAMO, a factor of 3.68. The attacker's receipts now represented about 55.51M MAMO, almost three times the cap on their own.

In parallel, the attacker's accounts bought about 94.31M MAMO on DEXs, including Aerodrome's MAMO/USDC pool, for about $7.5M of gross volume. Much of that was recycled borrowed money. The oracle feed climbed from $0.0106 at 09:06 to $0.4313 at 09:28 and was back near $0.014 by 09:45.

At Moonwell's highest accepted price, 55.51M MAMO was worth about $22.34M, which at a 50% collateral factor allowed about $11.17M of borrowing. The attacker took $11.03M. Certora makes the point that both halves were needed: without the donation the position stays at 15M MAMO, and without the pump 55M MAMO at $0.0106 is only worth about $590K.

Liquidators seized essentially all of the attacker's mMAMO across 595 liquidation events, but the MAMO price was already collapsing, so the seized collateral could not cover the debt. The attacker never needed to redeem the donated MAMO. Borrowing against it and leaving the debt behind was the whole plan.

Moonwell's cap lives in the Comptroller's mintAllowed hook. Certora quotes the check:

The formula is correct: it measures everything the market owes its suppliers, including donated cash. The problem is when it runs. It only runs on mint. A MAMO transfer executes inside the MAMO token contract and never calls Moonwell, so no Moonwell code can object. As Anthias put it, "the 20 million MAMO supply cap checked formal mint inputs." After the two transfers, the market would have refused any new deposit, but there was nothing left to refuse.

A cap enforced at one entry point only limits that entry point. If a quantity can also change through a path you do not control, the cap is a speed bump, not a limit.

Donation attacks on Compound forks are not new. Certora notes that Moonwell's own repository has carried a test since 2023 that reproduces the Hundred Finance exploit: it sends tokens directly to a market, and a comment says the attacker "can now borrow everything in the markets due to the massively inflated exchange rate." The tests then check that the donation cannot be pulled back out through redeemUnderlying. That protects one exit, but the MAMO attacker used a different one: borrowing.

In 2026 alone, Certora lists three Compound v2 forks hit by direct transfers combined with a pumped, thin collateral token: Venus on 15 March (where, per Rekt, a position reached 367% of the cap), Moonwell on 27 August and Tectonic on Cronos on 30 August. We touched on Tectonic's price manipulation in our roundup of recent blockchain hack lessons. The pattern is close to what happened in the Premia v3 vault exploit: the code did what it was written to do, but an accounting assumption about where balances come from did not hold.

The robust fix is to stop deriving cash from balanceOf. Certora proposes tracking cash in an internal ledger that only the market's own transfer functions move. A simplified version of their patch:

A live market would also need a one-time admin call to initialise the ledger to the current balance. Certora's AutoProver, run after the attack against commit 3b32d53 (the last before the attack), wrote a rule stating that a donation must not change the supplier claim the cap is checked against. The Certora Prover reports that rule violated on the deployed contract and verified with the ledger, assuming MAMO is a standard ERC-20 with no callbacks. Moonwell, for its part, has not changed how markets count cash; it set the MAMO supply and borrow caps to 1 wei, used about $246K of reserves to repay bad debt in the USDC market (MIP-X66), and set MAMO's collateral factor to 0% from 17 October (MIP-X69).

1. Never price shares from balanceOf(address(this)). Vault shares, lending receipts and LP tokens should all be valued from internal accounting. If you must read the balance, treat any excess as a donation that does not change share value. This belongs on every smart contract security checklist.

2. Enforce invariants on state, not on entry points. Ask "what can change this number?" rather than "which function should check it?". If a transfer can move it, the check has to live where the number is read, or the number has to stop depending on transfers.

3. Treat low-liquidity collateral as an oracle problem and a cap problem together. A cap sized to liquidation depth is only meaningful if nothing can grow positions past it. Pair caps with price feeds that resist minute-scale manipulation, such as TWAPs or circuit breakers on sudden moves.

4. Test the exits you did not think of. Moonwell tested that a donation could not be redeemed. It did not test that a donation could not be borrowed against. For each attack class, enumerate every way value can leave: redeem, borrow, liquidate, transfer receipts.

5. Monitor for unsolicited transfers. A 35M token transfer into a market contract with no Mint event is a loud, cheap signal. An alert on that would have given Moonwell about ten minutes before the final borrows.

The Moonwell exploit is a reminder that a correct check in the wrong place is not a control. The supply cap measured the right number, and the attack class had even been tested for years earlier, yet $11M walked out through a path nobody had pinned down. If your protocol values shares, receipts or collateral from token balances, talk to our team or see our audit pricing to have those accounting assumptions reviewed before someone tests them on mainnet.

#9759. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

MIC contract coverage of Transformers model types

#9758. I asked a chat app for a caching diagram. It drew the 304 as a 204.

Quick note first: I do marketing for HelloAI (tryhello.app), and this is a test I ran on its free plan. I'll show the prompt, the picture it gave me, and where it slipped.

Make an image: a simple sequence diagram of HTTP conditional caching. Two lanes only: Browser and Server. Four numbered arrows with SHORT labels: 1 GET /logo.png, 2 200 OK + ETag, 3 GET with If-None-Match, 4 304 Not Modified (no body). Large legible text, minimal words, flat style.

It took about a minute and returned one image (1536x1024):

The flow is the standard revalidation round trip. The browser asks for a file, the server answers 200 with an ETag, the browser asks again with If-None-Match, and the server answers 304 with no body. MDN's 304 page describes exactly this: it is sent for a conditional GET or HEAD with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since when the condition is false, and it must not contain a body. MDN 304

The arrow directions are right, the lanes are right, and the text is large and readable, which was not a given. A different prompt I tried yesterday (a water cycle infographic) came back with garbled labels in the part I could see, so I asked for fewer words this time on purpose.

I only caught the 204 because I compared the picture with my own prompt. If you generate diagrams like this, check every label.

A diagram you can see and fix is a better starting point than a paragraph, and the clean layout is the part that worked. But the one wrong status code in the middle is exactly the kind of error a pretty picture hides. One prompt, one run, nothing cherry-picked: this is the only image I made for this post.

#9756. Your Context Is the New Moat: Here's Why

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Jack Dorsey says there is no moat anymore. Yet, Palantir is up 668% in five years, Instinct is valued at $10 billion, and Emergent hit $100 million in annualized revenue in eight months. Both can’t be true unless the moat moved.

My bet: it moved to context. The software that wins from here will behave less like a tool and more like a consultant who knows your business deeply: one that tells you what to do, and then does much of it for you.

The cost of building software is collapsing, and agents can now do real work, so everyone is asking. Jack Dorsey (co-founder of Twitter and Square) says there is none; others say distribution is the moat, and Karri Saarinen (Linear CEO) argues that individual taste will always create moats.

https://x.com/jack/status/2114121702515114234

None of them won on the ability to build software. Technically, anyone can release an assistant; Instinct is still worth $10 billion. They won on knowing the customer’s world well enough to do the work, not just support it.

Palantir, built on embedding deeply in how each customer operates, is the clearest case:

The old moats were the ability to build software, owning the customer, and feature breadth with its integrations and switching costs. Now that software can be generated, the first and the last no longer count. The new moats are:

The difference matters. Code can be generated in an afternoon. Context can’t: it builds up from use, decisions, and outcomes, and it compounds.

You can already see the shift. Google Ads’ auto-applied recommendations adjust your campaigns based on your own account’s history, and Shopify Sidekick answers questions and takes actions using your store’s data.

If context is the moat, the practical question is where it lives. The agent world has quietly settled on an almost embarrassingly simple answer: plain Markdown files the agent reads before it acts. That’s the harness: the files, triggers, and tools around a model that decide what it knows and when it moves.

Look at OpenClaw, an open-source personal agent, or gstack, Garry Tan’s open-source Claude Code setup. Each file answers one question:

A chat, a schedule, or an event triggers the agent. It reads those files, then understands, acts, and checks, using tools like a browser, APIs, and code. The result is an answer or completed work.

For an online store, the harness comes down to five files. What makes them work is being specific. Here’s what they might say for a skincare brand:

Now put a harness like this inside a real store. On day one, it simply sets honest expectations: Sam’s first sale will usually take six to seven days.

By month two, it doesn’t wait to be asked. Sam’s Goals.md says returns should be under 4% by December; they’re at 5.8%. So it brings three questions worth asking, each with a “Research this” button.

And when there’s work to do, it says so: nine listings with reduced visibility, fourteen photos to fix, three listings flagged in reviews. Next to each one is a single button: Do it for me.

Start with the five files. Write down your goals, your principles, how your KPIs actually break down, the patterns you’ve already learned, and your users. Write them in plain Markdown, and keep them current.

That’s what turns software from a tool that runs a workflow into something closer to a high-powered consultant with very deep insight into your business: one that tells you what you should be doing, and then does a lot of it on your behalf.
