#9681. One Can Of Sweetened Condensed Milk Is The Start To This Easy Brazilian Dessert

Many desserts can be intimidatingly complex, requiring both difficult technique and extensive ingredients. That need not always be the case, though. For a delicious batch of brigadeiros – an iconic Brazilian dessert – preparation starts with a simple can of sweetened condensed milk. The sweet is essentially like a chewy chocolate truffle, constructed using a trio of cocoa powder, butter, and the cornerstone condensed milk. The assembly is as straightforward as the ingredients. All components are simmered together over low heat for around twenty minutes to thicken, then cooled and formed into bite-sized balls.

Although easy to make, the dessert is delicious and playful. The condensed milk lends each bite a signature caramel-like sweetness, balanced out by the cocoa bitterness. The dessert is made to a soft consistency, but often coated with fun garnishes like chocolate sprinkles, nuts, or coconut flakes, yielding an intriguing textural contrast. Arranged on a plate, it's a surprising way to use condensed milk with an impressive result.

With Brigidiaro's three-ingredient composition, every element plays a role in the final flavor. Not all cans of sweetened condensed milk are alike. Some taste sweeter, others more caramel-forward, all while varying in texture, too. As the sole source of sugar in the dessert, the type you choose defines its sweetness. For example, regular granulated sugar is a blank canvas, ready to take on the cocoa flavor while brown sugars have a little note of molasses. Want to fine-tune the brigidiaro even further? Consider making your own sweetened condensed milk at home using solely milk and sugar.

In parallel, the employed cocoa powder also makes a noticeable difference. The foodstuff's treatment influences the taste –  a Dutch process will feature less acidity, for example. And for even more control over the Brigidairo's chocolate taste, consider shaving a chocolate bar, one of the easiest substitutes for cocoa powder. With such an inclusion, you can vary the cocoa composition. An 85% cocoa powder will lend the brigidairo more complex dark and earthy notes, while a milder 50% makes for an extra sweet and creamy experience.

Butter serves as a fat that brings the components together. Go for a classic unsalted stick; there's no need for an extra flavorful cultured butter or a higher-fat European-style. And once the fat has melted, you could optionally stir in flavorings like lemon juice and zest (use white chocolate or skip it altogether for this) or spices such as nutmeg and cinnamon to add subtle warmth throughout your dessert. All held together with a three-ingredient foundation, brigadeiros welcome a multitude of subtle twists.

#9677. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9676. For Heartier Scrambled Eggs, Make Them Rolex-Style

Scrambled eggs make for a reliable breakfast option, but turning them into a hearty meal can be tricky. Sure, there's always the tried-and-true eggs on toast à la tartine, or a classic side of hash browns. However, to really shake up your breakfast routine, look toward the Ugandan rolex. This popular street food rolls up eggs into chapati (an unleavened flatbread), supplemented with flavorful vegetable additions. Wrapped up into a swirled shape, it's a dish reminiscent of a breakfast taco, only with an East African appeal all of its own.

Assembly starts like many an egg dish: The cornerstone ingredient is whisked in a bowl (although it can also be stirred in a pan for a change of texture). All the while, a variable vegetable medley consisting of ingredients like onion, tomatoes, spicy chiles, cabbage, and occasionally garlic softens in a pan. The eggs go into the veggie mix, are allowed to set, and are then rolled into already warmed flatbread.

Some construct the dish right in the pan; others on a separate plate. Either way, it's crucial to give the flatbread a tight roll — more than with a breakfast taco — creasing the dish over two to three times. Flavorful, handheld, and open to many modifications, a rolex (a play on the band of the watch and "rolled eggs") makes for a great addition to the morning rotation.

In Uganda — especially the capital, Kampala — rolex rolls are made by a multitude of vendors, each adding a unique spin. As a result, feel free to work in your own customizations, whether into the vegetable mix or as a condiment topping on top. Tomatoes, pepper, cabbage, and onion form the most frequent foundation, but you can also add carrots for textural enhancement. You can also enhance the flavor using aromatics like garlic, ginger, scallions, as well as fresh herbs like cilantro or parsley. You could even have an Asian-inspired riff and throw in some nori, chilli crunch, and mirin.

In addition to the vegetable filling, spiff out your rolex right before rolling. Opt for one of the cheeses that's a perfect addition to scrambled eggs for an ooey-gooey bite; Swiss or feta is a reliable choice. And to give the dish a more American flair, strips of bacon add to the heartiness. There's no such thing as too many components, so long as the roll stays intact. Traditionally, the dish is eaten handheld, wrapped in plastic on-the-go, so just make sure any additional ingredients sit securely in the eggs and flatbread.

#9675. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

#9673. Make Grilled Cheese Macedonian-Style For Double The Cheese & Flavor

Although less-famed than neighboring Greek and not-too-distant Turkish cooking, Northern Macedonian cuisine contains an abundance of delicious offerings. A mix of Balkan, Slavic, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern influences, there's a lot to take from this regional culinary style. You can even infuse a Macedonian flair into grilled cheese by making a dish called przeni lepcinja.

Reminiscent of French toast but with a distinctly Mediterranean flair, this meal makes for a savvy way to use stale bread. Thick slices of bread — typically sourdough — are soaked in an egg and milk mixture, then layered with a generous dose of shredded mozzarella in between. This sandwich is then pan-fried in aromatic olive oil, thereby forming a golden-brown, bready dish, stuffed with gooey cheese inside. Scattered with feta atop before serving, it's an international grilled cheese style worth trying.

After all, feta and eggs are a tried-and-true pairing; the cheese is salty and tangy and adds a complex dimension to breakfast food. Meanwhile, that interior mozz melts down into creamy-gooey goodness that's still quintessentially a grilled cheese. The dish comes together with pantry staples, but presents the elements in a creative new form.

The classic przeni lepcinja formula is delicious, but the dish welcomes other components, too. Cheese is an important part of Macedonian cuisine – as well as Balkan food broadly — so tracking down regional cheese varieties can give your przeni lepcinja an extra-flavorful flair. Look out for belo sirenje, a crumbly white cheese reminiscent of feta, but crafted according to Macedonian techniques. Often made with sheep's milk, you can substitute it with Greek Sheep Milk Feta, a product that's easier to find in the United States.

Don't rule out enhancing the Macedonian grilled cheese stuffing, either. Chop up some tomatoes and peppers for a touch of sweetness. Or add some ajvar, a relish made with roasted eggplants and bell peppers. The condiment is also popular in Macedonia, and oftentimes served alongside cheese. Finally, round out your przeni lepcinja with ham, which will add both salt and meatiness to the dish. If the components are difficult to fit alongside the mozzarella, scoop out some of the bread's interior — the egg binder will hold the sandwich together. Flavorful and easy-to-make, przeni lepcinja is worth including in the weeknight rotation.

Feelings of stress, fatigue, and exhaustion – what is being described as “burnout” – have become a common occurrence among providers, including rheumatologists, with important implications in clinical practice. Various surveys and studies have reported a substantial prevalence of burnout (approximately 50%) among rheumatology providers.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), joins us on this episode to provide deeper insight on the issue of “burnout” from a clinical practice standpoint.

Read the full transcript of the episode here.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, is the Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at UNC.

A recipient of a 2015 Rheumatology Research Foundation (RRF) Clinician Scholar Educator Award, Dr Jonas has developed a novel curriculum in Rheumatology in the Foundation Phase at UNC. She is a clinician educator and has an active rheumatology practice, where she sees patients with a wide spectrum of inflammatory rheumatic disorders. She teaches rheumatology to medical students, residents, and fellows and is actively involved in curricular development to train both physicians and advance practice providers in rheumatology.

Dr Jonas currently serves on the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Workforce Solutions Committee. She has previously served as the chair of the ACR Committee on Training and Workforce and has served as co-chair of the ACR In-Training Examination Taskforce. She has served on the board of the Rheumatology Research Foundation as well as the RRF Scientific Advisory Committee.

Dr Jonas is a founding member of the Carolinas Fellows Collaborative (CFC), a group of program directors from the Carolinas who work to enhance the education of their collective trainees. Dr Jonas was honored as the ACR Distinguished Rheumatology Program Director in 2015.

#9668. The Best Non-Traditional Chain Restaurant Reuben Sandwich, According To Customers

Reuben sandwiches, a throwback from the 1950s, are as closely linked to St. Patrick's Day as shamrocks and pots of gold, but you certainly don't have to wait until the March holiday to enjoy the salty, cheesy bite. There are, in fact, a number of chain restaurants that have Reubens on their menus year round, and in fact, Food Republic did a round-up of the 10 very best. Among the Arby's option, with its New York-style recipe, and Culver's grilled version, stuffed with meat, there is one standout choice that actually isn't super traditional, but customers love it anyway, and it's from Schlotzsky's Deli.

The Texas-based sandwich shop, which first opened its doors in 1971 has since grown to include nearly 300 locations across the U.S. This tasty Reuben is on the restaurant's permanent menu and what sets it apart from all the others is the bread. You see, while it has all the other markings of a classic Reuben, like pastrami, melted Swiss, a heap of sauerkraut, and Thousand Island Dressing (the other traditional option is Russian dressing, which is a little spicier), customers have the option of eating these ingredients on the chain's signature round sourdough. One reviewer on Google even proclaimed that they drive 40 minutes to get to the nearest Schlotzsky's to get its Reuben on this tangy white bread.

The deli sandwich chain does offer a rye option, which the customers love. But even Schlotzsky's dark rye bread is different from classic rye.

Schlotzsky's bread is so special that the Food Republic article cited customers as raving about it almost separate from all the fillings in its sandwiches. And the reason is simple: Unlike, say, McDonald's, whose English muffins are shipped in from a variety of regional bakeries, Schlotzsky's bread is baked fresh daily, in-house, and the employees do not cut any corners. Just like at home, the loaves at this chain must rise, proof, and then finally bake, in a process that takes about an hour (it is speeded up a bit by the use of in-kitchen proofers, which can accelerate the entire procedure).

But it's not just the freshness of the bread, it's also the ingredients, namely the proprietary sourdough starter that forms the basis of every bread the restaurant offers, from its Harvest Wheat, to the pizza crusts, and yes, even its rye bread. This is one part of what makes the Reuben from Schlotzsky's nontraditional, because aside from the fact that you can choose any of the chain's breads to fill with pastrami, cheese, sauerkraut and dressing, if you do opt for the rye bread, it isn't a classic, dense rye. Rather, it falls in line with the chain's sourdough, which is crispy on the outside but airy and tender on the inside, and is baked in a distinctive round shape.

#9667. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9665. The Spicy Sauce That Turns Beef Sandwiches Into A Baltimore Classic

There are plenty of reasons to take a trip to Baltimore; perhaps you're a fan of Old Bay seasoning and want to visit the place where its story began, or maybe you're eager to try Maryland's world-famous blue crabs. While Baltimore certainly doesn't lack options when it comes to seafood, the state is also home to a seriously impressive sandwich: pit beef. Made with thinly sliced, smoky roast beef piled onto a kaiser roll along with raw white onions, no pit beef is complete without a generous dollop of spicy tiger sauce.

Baltimore tiger sauce, a controversial inductee amongst regional barbecue sauces, requires just two core ingredients: mayonnaise and horseradish. Lemon juice, garlic, salt, and pepper are also common additions. Thanks to the horseradish, the sauce brings a different kind of burn than you get from chili peppers. When the root is grated or crushed, naturally occurring compounds called glucosinolates break down into pungent substances, including allyl isothiocyanate, which stimulates the same sensory receptors responsible for the sharp, biting sensation you get from wasabi — you know, the kind that hurts in the best way possible.

This sharp pungency helps cut through the richness of the smoky beef, and it's a great example of how a sandwich made with just a smattering of ingredients can still deliver complex flavors without needing to be piled high with a mismatch of toppings. A fresh batch can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to two days, and you can use it for more than just pit beef sandwiches; try spreading it on other roast beef sandwiches, serving it alongside steak, or using it as a dipping sauce for fries when regular old mayo just isn't cutting it.

If you don't want your nose tingling and your eyes watering the entire time you're eating your pit beef, you'll need to go easy on the horseradish. Even a small amount packs a hefty punch, especially when fresh. For a milder, more manageable kick, reach for prepared horseradish instead. This condiment is made from freshly grated or ground horseradish root mixed with vinegar and salt, and pairing it with mayo helps tame some of its harsh pungency. As a frame of reference, start without about one tablespoon of prepared horseradish for every quarter cup of mayonnaise, then taste and gradually add more until you reach your preferred level of punchiness.

But there's one element even more important than the tiger sauce, and that's the beef itself. There's plenty of debate over which cut works best, although most roads lead to either top round or bottom round. Both come from the cow's hindquarters, making them relatively lean cuts that are well-suited to pit beef. Traditionally, the meat is cooked over a hot charcoal fire, developing that smoky, browned crust while the inside stays pink and juicy. At home, a gas grill or even a hot cast iron skillet can get the job done if you don't have a charcoal grill handy.

Since these cuts don't have much fat to keep them moist, take care not to overcook them, or you'll end up with tough, dry beef. Once the roast has rested, grab the sharpest knife you own and slice the beef as thinly as possible (always against the grain). Those wafer-thin slices are key to getting that signature Baltimore pit beef sandwich texture.

#9663. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

#9660. Scrambled Eggs Get A Protein And Flavor Boost When You Add This Mediterranean Twist

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Scrambled eggs may be a simple day-to-day food, but they nevertheless welcome plenty of genius tricks to make them even better. A particularly savvy way to upgrade the dish is to turn it Mediterranean, mixing in spinach and feta for a reimagined egg dish. You'll get an herbal, lightly earthy touch from the spinach, and a salty-tangy flavor from the feta. The former will wilt into the eggs, the latter will soften, and together the two form an upgraded scrambled egg rendition.

Plus, in addition to a mouth-watering flavor boost, the add-ons up the protein content, too. According to the USDA, a single large egg contains just over 6 grams of protein, while a cup of feta has 21 grams of protein. A standard serving of the dish would contain about two eggs and roughly an ounce of feta, rounding out to approximately 16 grams of protein total if, say, you use a serving of something like Athenos Traditional Feta. Plus, the USDA states that a serving of mature spinach (about 85 grams) adds another 2.5 grams.

The two ingredients are easy to incorporate into scrambled eggs. You'll want to saute the spinach first using a fat like olive oil or butter, and then add the eggs. Feel free to stir the eggs before pouring them into the pan, or go with a Gordon Ramsay no-whisk style scrambled egg. Only once the eggs are nearing your preferred level of doneness, sprinkle in the feta — some even add the cheese once the pan is off the heat. The dairy will melt quickly, rounding out this tasty Mediterranean upgrade.

Spinach and feta alone make for a delicious scrambled egg rendition. However, the two ingredients also open the door to a wider array of Mediterranean influences, ready to revamp your breakfast experience. Enhancements can start simple. Use a high-quality extra virgin olive oil, thereby lending the dish a peppery or grassy complexity. You can also imbue some sweetness into the dish by caramelizing red or white onions before you wilt your spinach.

For a more drastic reinterpretation, consider taking inspiration from the Greek dish strapatsada (aka kagianas), which utilizes grated tomatoes alongside feta. Simmered down, the fruit lends eggs a satisfying sweetness. Top it with a serving of plain nonfat Greek yogurt, and you'll add another 17 grams of protein. Including bell peppers and pepper flakes brings the dish closer to menemen, a traditional Turkish breakfast dish. Both recipes pair fabulously with accouterments like olives, sliced cucumbers, and a rustic bread, say, a sliced ciabatta. It's a breakfast with a distinct Mediterranean character, all while using pantry staples.

#9657. A Nasty Sign Of Omega-3 Deficiency

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

Stiffness in the joints and swelling can be indirect signs of omega-3 deficiency, research suggests.

Waking up stiff in the morning, feeling pain in the joints, swelling, tenderness and loss of flexibility are all signs of arthritis.

Omega-3 deficiency could be contributing, as scientists believe there is a link between this leading cause of disability and a lack of omega-3 in the diet.

Researchers suggest that a diet rich in omega-3 could decrease the symptoms of osteoarthritis.

A study has found that adding fish oil to the diet — and to some degree flaxseed oil (alpha-linolenic acid has an anti-inflammatory effect) — can ease or even prevent osteoarthritis.

With population aging, osteoarthritis will be one of the leading causes of disability.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, by 2040 it is estimated that 26% of US adults aged 18 or older will be diagnosed by a doctor with arthritis.

While there are still no effective medications for treating this condition, omega-3 fish oil can be one of the best natural remedies in treating osteoarthritis.

Professor John Tarlton, the lead researcher of the study, explained the effect of omega-3 on osteoarthritis:

“Classic early signs of the condition, such as the degradation of collagen in cartilage and the loss of molecules that give it shock-absorbing properties, were both reduced with omega-3.

Furthermore, there was strong evidence that omega-3 influences the biochemistry of the disease, and therefore not only helps prevent disease, but also slows its progression, potentially controlling established osteoarthritis.”

Western diets contain high levels of omega-6 fatty acids, which can lead to inflammatory disorders such as colitis, heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.

Modern diets contain up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3, whereas our ancestor’s diets contained almost an equal level of these two omega fatty acids.

Therefore, supplementation with omega-3 can help to restore this imbalance in Western diets and improve conditions such as colitis and heart-related diseases.

Fish oil is much more effective than flax seed oil, but for vegetarians and vegans this supplement is an important option.

“Most diets in the developed world are lacking in omega-3, with modern diets having up to 30 times too much omega-6 and too little omega-3.

Taking omega-3 will help redress this imbalance and may positively contribute to a range of other health problems such as heart disease and colitis.”

The study was published in the journal of Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (Knott et al., 2011).

#9655. Not Butter Or Mayo: Roasted Potatoes Are 10x Richer With One Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Crafting a top-tier batch of roasted potatoes is often harder than it seems — there are many mistakes everyone tends to make. A detail that's especially commonly overlooked is the employed fat. The type you use doesn't only help crisp up your spuds, but it can be transformative for the overall texture and taste. With that in mind, ditch classic options like olive oil or butter, and look to French and British tradition and opt for duck fat instead. It's an easy way to add mouth-watering richness and remarkable crunch, all without perceptible duck-like flavors.

Often used in European cuisine, duck fat lands on the obscure side in American cooking. Tracking down the foodstuff isn't too difficult, though. You can grab a can of Rendered Duck Fat for Cooking on Amazon, grab some from Walmart, as well as peruse your local farmer's market. A huge quantity isn't necessary: A quarter cup is suitable for three pounds of potatoes.

Once procured, melt the duck fat before adding to a roast, using either a stovetop or microwave for gentle softening. Combine the fat with optional aromatics, then coat the potatoes, and roast away. You'll get a tray of uber-crispy spuds, enhanced with an extra decadent touch, that will stay crispy.

Duck fat alone establishes a strong character for roast potatoes, meaning you won't need many additional components to round out the dish. It's common — but not essential – to incorporate flour or semolina for the crispiest roast potatoes. The starch binds with the fat and seasonings to create an extra crispy external layer, lending the dish an added textural touch. Alternatively, some boil the potatoes in baking soda before roasting, a savvy technique that produces an extra soft spud interior. Or you can take a tip from British roasted potatoes and parboil, then shake your spuds before they get roasted.

In addition to the potato consistency, there are also potential seasonings to consider. A generous sprinkling of salt is a must, pepper is strongly encouraged, and further ingredients are to personal taste. Garlic roasted potatoes are a tried-and-true classic, as are tubers flavored with rosemary or thyme. You can also add a single bay leaf for herbal complexity, or finish with a sprinkle of parmesan for a cheesy touch. If you're running low on duck fat — or craving a potato rendition that's less rich — feel free to cut the ingredient with olive oil. However, you won't want to leave the ingredient out altogether: Duck fat is roast potato magic.

#9651. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

#9649. Forget Takeout: Customers Love These Frozen Mexican Foods

If you're lucky, you live just a short ride away from a half dozen quality Mexican restaurants serving bubbling bowls of pozole, punchy tacos, and sultry stews of slow-cooked meats. But not everyone lives in communities blessed with quality Mexican cooking. And that's a major bummer, because this regional cuisine is simply electric, balancing deep flavors with fresh herbs, warm spices, and piquant chiles. Mexican food plays with different textures and shapes, allowing you to compose bites that are simultaneously creamy and crisp, cool and spicy, savory and sweet.

Thankfully, you can enjoy decent Mexican and Tex-Mex-inspired food from the comfort of your couch. And all it takes is a trip to your local supermarket. First, let's preface this entire article by saying that a good restaurant will almost always outdo a frozen dupe. Still, there is something to be said for the convenience and cost savings of air-frying a chimichanga or microwaving a burrito for lunch. I turned to the internet to find frozen Mexican meals comparable to what you might get at a restaurant or fast-casual takeout spot. After sorting through hundreds of reviews and comments, I put together a list of the top customer-favorite Mexican appetizers, sides, and main meals available in the freezer aisle.

The foundation of a good tamale is corn, specifically corn that's been soaked in an alkaline solution (AKA nixtamalized), which transforms the dense starchy kernels into a pliable, dough-like carbohydrate called masa. Making masa (and tamales) requires time, skill, precision, and technique. But if you don't possess any of the above, then heating up a frozen tamale is your best option.

There are a surprising number of choices in this department, but customers are especially fond of the Trader Joe's versions. Like many Trader Joe's items, people gripe that these come in and out of stock with about as much predictability as a June weather forecast. However, the cheese and green chile and the chicken and cheese varieties are consistently the most reliable (and available). Tamales make a good side dish, especially if you want an alternative to potatoes or pasta, or, like one Redditor, you can steam one and bring it for lunch. A negative is that since they have to be reheated, the masa interior can get a tad dry. To remedy this, Trader Joe's shoppers recommend a side of salsa, hot sauce, guacamole, rice and beans, or a blanket of extra melted cheese.

As far as frozen Mexican entrées go, the burrito bowl can be controversial. Why? Unlike a tamale, chimichanga, or taquito, a burrito bowl doesn't require the same finesse, so customers generally expect a higher quality product. Surprisingly, many reliable brands struggle to execute what seems like a simple dish. But not Kevin's Natural Foods. If unfamiliar, Kevin's positions itself as a better-for-you frozen meal. Ingredients are clean, non-GMO, and gluten-free. These restrictions are far from a hindrance. On the contrary, the quality of Kevin's frozen meals, especially its burrito bowls, is top-notch.

At least, that's what the customers say. "Absolutely loaded with cheese, chicken in every bite, rice perfectly cooked, veggies still have a bit of a snap to them, and the chipotle sauce has a ton of flavor," one Redditor commented. Others shared a similar opinion. With Kevin's, there's a general appreciation for the quality and portion size. The brand doesn't skimp on proteins or portion size, and whatever ingredients are included are thoughtfully prepared — no mushy rice, sad veggies, or gloopy cheese. The result keeps customers happy.

Many culinary historians consider mole the national dish of Mexico. The sauce's dynamic flavors mirror the country's history: dark and complex, with an underlying sweetness and grounding depth. Mole requires dozens of Mexico's most prized indigenous ingredients — chocolate, chiles, nuts, seeds, spices — to create something that's, frankly, unmatched in any other cuisine.

Does Trader Joe's version capture that centuries of Mexican culinary tradition? That would be impossible. However, given its price and unbelievable convenience, it does a pretty good job of imitating the sweet-and-savory balance of a traditional mole. With just one package, you can make multiple meals. And while a traditional mole takes hours — if not days — to prepare, TJ's frozen chicken mole takes just minutes in the microwave.

The taste is bold, but the texture of the chicken — not overly mushy or stringy — makes it ideal for several applications. Customers say they use it to fill enchiladas and tacos, but you can use it for everything from pizza to nachos to an omelet.

Known for its better-for-you ingredient profile, Amy's has been supplying organic frozen entrées for decades. While some frozen tortilla-wrapped items suffer from a textural breakdown, the tortillas housing Amy's enchilada filling hold up well. All of Amy's frozen entrées are vegetarian-friendly, but where they lack in meat, they make up for it in texture, flavor, and composition. Amy's cheese enchiladas have been a hit with shoppers for decades, with the blend of cheeses, toasty corn tortillas, and savory tomato-based enchilada sauce, and they still earn online praise today.

"I find these to have an incredible depth of flavor for a frozen meal," began one Redditor's review. "I would be 100% happy if this was served to me in a restaurant." Others say that the product is the best in frozen food. And while there's no question that shoppers have enjoyed and appreciated the taste of Amy's foods for years, they are a bit disgruntled about the ever-increasing price point. And while that might be on the higher end of the price spectrum, anything in the $7 or $8 range for a frozen meal does seem a little steep. But they're still beloved, despite that.

The taquito was created as a thrifty way to use up leftover tortillas and filling. Little did its creators know that the fried, toasty snack would become widely beloved happy marriage of taste, form, and texture. Taquitos are almost always made from corn tortillas and filled with everything from chicken and cheese to beef, veggies, and beans. But the best part of a taquito is its tubular shape that's seemingly designed for dipping.

Frozen taquitos aren't new, and their basic composition hasn't changed much over the years. You'll find a plethora of options in the freezer aisle, but customers are most fond of El Monterey's Extra Crunchy Southwest Chicken variety. Fans say it's hard to eat just one... or two. Shoppers also love its unique exterior crust.

The only downside to El Monterey's taquitos is the quantity of filling. There's a collective sigh at how the interiors have grown increasingly barren over the years, an observation noticeable in the chicken taquitos, where the chicken and vegetables retain their individual shapes, unlike the beef and bean option, which is more of a paste. An easy solution is to prepare a few different dips — sour cream, guacamole, queso — to add extra moisture and unctuousness.

If a taquito and a burrito had a baby, it would be a chimichanga. It's deep-fried, which ups the richness but also gives the tortilla a crispy shell that's the ideal foil for any smooth refried bean or cheese filling. Deep frying at home doesn't require the same precision as making a chocolate soufflé, but it still means more work and cleanup than simply reheating on a hot frying pan. That's why a good frozen chimichanga is crucial if you suddenly get that itch for this fried Tex-Mex specialty. And, again, the El Monterey brand delivers.

Online, there was a lot of love for El Monterey, saying it has some of the best frozen burritos and chimichangas on the market. Unlike the taquitos, the chimichangas have a generous filling that, as one person put it, is comparable to the reference photo on the bag. The key to executing these properly is in the preparation. The chimichanga is inherently greasy, so a quick thaw in the microwave followed by a crisp-up on a hot pan usually does the trick. An air-fryer works, too. Some people just throw them in the deep fryer because, well, why not?

The burrito is the quintessential frozen Mexican food item, and over the decades, dozens — if not hundreds — of brands have battled each other for category supremacy. Many have faltered, but a handful have held their ground. Like Red's. Founded in 2009, Red's focuses on one thing: burritos. Sure, it'll try a breakfast sandwich or a "Snacker," but its product lineup is mostly just an array of tortilla-wrapped goodies.

Customers are big fans of the steak and cheddar burrito. While other cheaper, mass-market frozen burritos rely on mushy, indistinguishable fillings, Red's has made a name for itself by using higher-quality ingredients. Although shoppers are big fans of Red's entire line of burritos, they do gripe about the prices. Heating the burrito is another issue entirely, but one Red's expert has a foolproof method: Run it under water in the sink for a few seconds before microwaving. The extra moisture makes the tortilla a bit springier and more pliable. Wrapping it in a wet paper towel will have a similar effect.

The Mexican Style Street Corn Triangles from Tastiez are far from traditional Mexican cuisine. Instead, they are a frozen food product inspired by the classic Mexican street food esquites, which is like a bolder, saltier version of creamed corn. Another way to think of it is like elote, that yummy, cheese-dusted ear of grilled corn, stripped off the cob.

This product is a major departure from the original dish, but if you're craving an easy appetizer inspired by an authentic Mexican dish, it's not such a bad substitute. And, most importantly (at least for this article), customers have given these fried, corn-filled triangles their seal of approval. Whereas your average stuffed, fried snack oozes its insides after a hard bake or big bite, these stay pretty much intact. The crisp outside and gooey center make for a satisfying finger food, but it's the taste that brings it home, with reviewers gushing over its delicious street corn flavor. They come out best when deep-fried, but the air-fryer is an excellent alternative that still yields a crisp exterior.

Today, you can find the most elaborate culinary delights in your supermarket freezer. But while brands can execute everything from frozen kimbap to cioppino, many still struggle to nail a good frozen taco. What has customers complaining is the ratio of filling to shell: not enough of the former and too much of the latter, resulting in a product that's dry and brittle. Maybe tacos are difficult to seal, so manufacturers are forced to under fill? Whatever the reason, some brands miss the mark, while others, like Don Miguel, lead by example.

The Don Miguel Chicken Chipotle Mini Tacos have an active and passionate Reddit community that few items on this list can match. But why? What makes this 50-pack of frozen tacos from Costco so special? The price and crave-worthiness. However, while the consensus is generally positive, long-time customers have commented that the tacos are a bit spicier than they used to be. For this issue, the main workaround is a cooling condiment, like Greek yogurt or sour cream. Still, although people do love these things, it seems like the perfect mini taco has yet to be discovered.

The churro is one of the most globally recognized Mexican desserts. It's basically a twist or extruded wand of fried dough that's tossed in cinnamon sugar and served with, if you're lucky, a smooth chocolate sauce or caramel. Churros come in many shapes and sizes. Costco, famous for scaling everything to the max, sells a foot-long version in its food court for just $1.49. But if you want to scratch that churro itch at home, you can pick up a pack of Hola Churros.

No, these aren't as long as the ones you'll find in the food court, but some regular Costco customers think they're just smaller versions of the same make and model. But how do they taste? Overall, shoppers are pretty pleased. Are they as crisp and pleasantly oily as the ones you'll find at a street fair or Mexican restaurant? Probably not. But they do the job. The key is finding ways to deliver that extra punch of flavor. Although they come with individual packs of cinnamon sugar, some Redditors recommend drizzling chocolate on them. They're also good as a topping for an ice cream sundae. For heating, skip the microwave and go for the air-fryer or toaster oven. No matter how you make them, they are an unbelievably good value: around $14.49 for a box of 30.

When you see a chile relleno on the menu at a Mexican restaurant, it's worth getting. This dish is pretty special, integrating all the different tastes and flavors that make cuisine from this part of the world so interesting and seductive. It's essentially a cheese-stuffed pepper that's battered, fried, and served on top of a rich tomato sauce. It takes some work to prepare, but it's a real stunner when it hits the table.

Somehow the team at Trader Joe's has managed to capture all these dynamic tastes and textures in one convenient, easy-to-heat frozen package. The batter is tempura-style, somewhat spongy but not in a soggy way, providing heft and unctuousness to the otherwise bare, roasted pepper wrapper. The cheese is pleasantly rubbery, and the sauce is savory and delicious. On Reddit, customers are surprised by how good it tastes, even despite the soft, slightly mushy texture. Of all the foods on this list, this one had the most overwhelmingly positive score for flavor. The consensus is that you should reheat the peppers in the air-fryer, not the microwave. Overall, people think the flavor is fantastic, and for just $5.99, you really can't go wrong.

Although this brand of Trader Joe's frozen rice is called "Spanish-style," its flavor profile is decidedly Mexican, drawing on spices and ingredients indigenous to Central America. Tomato gives it its mellow orange color, and a savory spice blend and quick toasting add an umami undertone that makes it easy to pair with dishes from across the culinary landscape, from madras lentils to gyros.

On Reddit, Trader Joe's faithful say it's an excellent accompaniment to many of the store's frozen and refrigerated Mexican entrées, like the birria, mole, green chili and cheese tamales, and even the salad kits. Others use it as a quick and flavorful foundation to a dish. Its utility is what makes this product so special. With dozens of comments on one Reddit thread dedicated to the Spanish-style rice, you can find dozens of interesting and inventive use cases. And while it's marketed as a microwavable grain, some shoppers are convinced you get a better result when you toast it in a pan.

First, I identified some of the more popular Mexican dishes that come frozen. From there, I explored different brands, and using Reddit, Facebook, and other social media channels, I got a sense of which products performed best.

For example, the top taquito maker didn't necessarily deliver the best burrito. I wanted to present a variety, so I didn't repeat dishes. It was difficult to find the top flavor(s), so when there wasn't a clear consensus, I tended to go with the one with the most feedback and attention.

#9648. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9645. Pickle Juice Vs Buttermilk: Which Marinade Is Best For Fried Chicken?

When it comes to down-home Southern cooking, buttermilk and pickles both have a prominent place thanks to their flavors and how they affect the chemistry of cooking. Todd Johnson, Proprietor of Strips Chicken & Brewing, insists that both have a place in fried chicken — although he asserts that buttermilk is the better all-around choice.

"If you're going to marinate your chicken, buttermilk wins," Johnson told Food Republic. "It's gently acidic, so it softens the surface of the chicken without turning it mushy. It's also thick enough to leave a tacky layer that flour clings to. That's the foundation of a craggy, crunchy crust." Just about any marinade can infuse the muscle fibers with moisture and keep it more tender, but it's that combination of subtle acid, sugars, and milk solids that gives it a more well-rounded, heartier flavor and makes it such an essential ingredient in fried chicken. Since it lacks the potency of a pickle brine, it also tends to absorb other seasonings quite well, so you don't have to rely solely on your breading.

While Johnson admits to being "not a fan of pickle juice as a marinade," he noted that it can have its place. "It's already salty and acidic, so it seasons and moistens the meat quickly," he explained. "You'll notice results in a couple of hours instead of overnight." Still, its high acidity means you have a narrower window between tender and mushy chicken, so it's not an ideal choice for beginners. Brine is a pretty potent ingredient, so while it's effective, it also calls for an experienced hand unless you're willing to experiment.

Good fried chicken has three components: meat, breading, and oil. Buttermilk is such a mainstay in recipes because it has a delicious effect on all three of these, promoting flavor, browning, and texture.

One of many major mistakes everyone makes with fried chicken is creating a breading that doesn't stick, and dry ingredients aren't the only contributor to this. "Oil and fat act like a release agent between meat and crust," Todd Johnson explained. "That's why we use fat-free buttermilk." For this aspect, it may seem like pickle brine is the right choice, but Johnson said that its lack of fat comes at the cost of a thinner consistency. Fat-free buttermilk is far more adhesive, giving your dry ingredients a prime surface to cling to, so they won't fall off the meat once they hit the oil.

Johnson conceded that buttermilk has a tendency to "over-brown" if your oil gets too hot, burning the milk sugars and solids, fouling the flavor. This is a pretty hefty disadvantage, but one that can be turned to an advantage with a careful eye. If you maintain Johnson's recommended oil temperature of 350 degrees Fahrenheit, you can toast, rather than burn, those solids, delivering a robust flavor profile focused on a hearty, umami-rich breading. Buttermilk is also a more convenient option, as you can just remove the excess drippings and drop your meat directly into your breading.

When you're looking to make fried chicken on the fly or don't have a surplus of seasoning, there are few options better than pickle brine. Todd Johnson said it's indispensable for achieving that "sandwich shop flavor" that some folks prefer, even if it has its quirks.

While you can always add some salt to your buttermilk, it won't have quite the same effect as using a jar of leftover pickle brine. "It's already salty and acidic, so it seasons and moistens the meat quickly," Todd Johnson clarified. Its extremely high and well-dissolved sodium content loosens up muscle fibers, making them far better at retaining moisture. While it lacks the rich solids and sugars of buttermilk, it brings far more tang, so it'll cut through even the heartiest, most marbled pieces of fried meat quite easily.

The biggest downside to pickle juice in your marinade is inconsistency and lack of other seasoning options. Not all brines are made the same, so unless you work with the exact same brand and product every time, there's always some amount of guess work involved. While pickle juice is one of the most powerful vehicles for flavor, it also leaves very little room for anything more subtle or nuanced. After marinating your meat, you'll also need to carefully pat dry each piece before tossing it in a batter or dry ingredients. Excess surface moisture creates a steam barrier between your chicken and breading, so even a bit left on the surface can ruin your food.

#9644. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

#9642. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9639. Skip Expensive Sea Bass: The Cheaper Fish Alternative With More Omega-3

It's never a bad idea to get more seafood into your diet. It's a great source of protein, loaded with a whole alphabet of nutrients, and most importantly, it's reliably delicious. There's an endless variety of seafood to suit any taste, and one fish many shoppers reach for is Chilean sea bass; however, anyone familiar with it knows it rarely comes cheap. If you're in the market for something rich and buttery without the sky-high price, sablefish is an excellent alternative.

Sablefish, commonly known as black cod, is a deep-water fish native to the North Pacific, ranging from Mexico to Alaska and the Bering Sea. Despite the name, it isn't a true cod, just as Chilean sea bass isn't a true bass. Both are white fish, a category usually associated with lean flesh, but these two are the exception to the rule. Because they live in cold, deep waters, they store plenty of omega-3-rich fat. But that doesn't make them equal. In fact, sablefish outranks not only sea bass but virtually any other whitefish when it comes to omega-3 content.

Its famously high fat content gives sablefish its indulgently rich, buttery texture and juicy flavor. For reference, salmon is the fish most people associate with omega-3s, and sablefish lands in the same ballpark with practically the same amounts (per Oregon State University). Surprisingly, despite being the richer option of the two whitefish, it tends to come in considerably cheaper than pricey Chilean sea bass, with strong catches and population booms strongly contributing to its more approachable price point.

Though sablefish is generally more affordable than Chilean sea bass, that doesn't necessarily mean it's budget-friendly. It remains a favorite at high-end restaurants, and one of the most famous examples is Nobu. At this Japanese-Peruvian fusion spot beloved by celebrities, miso-marinated black cod is one of its signature dishes. Fortunately, you can recreate this viral favorite at home without paying an arm or a leg.

Simply leave the fillets in a mixture of miso paste, mirin, sake, and sugar for at least two hours, or ideally overnight, to let the flavors work their way into the fish. When you're ready to cook, scrape off the excess marinade and broil the fish for around seven minutes, until the surface is beautifully caramelized and lightly charred while the inside remains tender and buttery. Pair that with some sushi rice made Chef Nobu style for a Michelin-worthy dinner all from the comfort of your own home.

When it comes to cooking, sablefish sets itself apart from the cod it shares its name with thanks to its high fat content. Your standard Atlantic or Pacific cod is exceptionally lean, making it protein-dense but also a little trickier to cook without drying out. Black cod, meanwhile, is far more forgiving when it comes to heat. Its generous fat content helps protect the flesh from drying out, even when exposed to high temperatures, making it an excellent candidate for a wide range of cooking methods, from pan-searing and grilling to broiling, roasting, pan-frying, and even smoking.

#9637. Turn Wendy's Chili Into Game Day Nacho Dip With This Ex-Employee's Simple Hack

Wendy's menu includes many items you might expect to find at a fast food joint: burgers (although it uniquely offers square patties), fries, chicken nuggets, and salads. But the chain is also a standout in the drive-thru world, as it's one of the few major brands to offer customers items like baked potatoes and bowls of chili, the latter of which are truly comforting after a long day when you want something hearty and filling. Wendy's chili can also be useful on game day as the base for a single-serve nacho dip, and all you have to do is add nacho cheese and sour cream.

The creator of this hack — a former Wendy's employee — simply adds the two extra ingredients and gives it a thorough stir, so it's an incredibly easy upgrade to pull off. Both the nacho cheese and the sour cream will mix easily into the chili, provided it's still hot, or at least warm, from the restaurant, with the cheese adding richness and the sour cream lending a welcome tang. Together, they also create a creamier consistency that makes it perfect for dipping.

If it has cooled, you might want to give it a quick nuke in the microwave (in a different vessel). If it's not quite nacho-y enough for your tastes, you can absolutely sprinkle in some smoky taco seasoning. Or dress it up with some diced jalapeños for heat, and top it with green onions to cut through all the richness.

#9636. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9635. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!
